items.statement: The task force reached consensus on 11 recommendations for emerging good practice and on 12 prioritised future research recommendations, from 14 good practice and 11 future research items put to the first-round vote.

values.denominator: 14 proposed good practice recommendations voted on in round one

items.statement: SHEER recommends that family and caregiver health spillovers be included in economic evaluations conducted from a healthcare/health payer perspective as well as from more inclusive societal or public sector perspectives.

The recommended aggregation procedure is stepwise: estimate spillovers among specified caregivers and family members or for the closest and second closest network members; report patient and caregiver/family QALY gains and losses separately; aggregate spillovers with patient effects by additive summation; and supplement the reference case with sensitivity analysis using wider or narrower networks.

Equal weighting should be applied to patient and family/caregiver health impacts unless empirical evidence shows that the decision maker or society values them differently in the context under investigation.

Collection of primary spillover data is currently preferred, with clear justification required when secondary data are used; the evidence review found trial-based evaluations more often used primary data while models relied on secondary data.

Outcome measurement should follow the jurisdiction's health technology assessment guidelines unless another method is empirically shown to be more appropriate, should ideally use the same measure for patients and spillover recipients when outcomes are to be aggregated, and should otherwise consider cost-consequence analysis.

Consensus was not reached on two proposed recommendations: using empirical exchange rates to convert care-related quality of life measures such as the Carer Experience Scale or CarerQol into health-related quality of life outcomes such as EQ-5D, and presenting spillover and patient effects as a multiplier applied to the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio; no proposed recommendation was judged inappropriate.

The highest priority future research avenues were exploring the distributional consequences of spillovers, adopting longitudinal study designs, and examining joint patient-caregiver utility elicitation methods; the lowest ranked were reporting bias and elicitation of social value weights.

values.subgroup: Development of novel generic preference-based measures for spillovers (rank 10)

items.statement: Analysts should consider and discuss the risk of double counting given the measurement technique used, flagging it as a source of uncertainty or bias, and should characterise and present uncertainty around spillover estimates, preferably by applying probability distributions to model parameters such as caregiver utility within probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Patient and caregiver contributors favoured inclusion of health spillovers in economic evaluations and particularly endorsed a time horizon long enough to capture impacts occurring remote to the caregiving experience, and additive summation across the family network.

The recommendations are intended as an initial roadmap rather than a strict checklist, to motivate wider incorporation of health spillovers and to stimulate public discussion and innovation while the evidence base develops.

Globally standardised methods of incorporation are neither realistic nor desirable; balance is needed between consistency where valuable for decision making and variation reflecting different decision maker perspectives, with transparent reporting of assumptions, data sources and methods being the essential common element.

A theme of principle versus practicability pervaded the discussions, since ideal practice is often infeasible under data constraints; adding an item to the CHEERS 2022 checklist could formalise disclosure of barriers to spillover incorporation.

A registry or tariff of spillover utilities and disutilities was discussed as a way to support incorporation where prospective data cannot be collected and to help establish an average spillover for displaced activity.

The guidance represents the consensus view of a purposively sampled group of subject-matter experts, and acceptance of invitations may have produced a group sharing the view that inclusion of spillovers is important.
No members from Latin America participated, so practices and implications of spillover incorporation in that and other regions remain poorly understood.

The scope was restricted to spillovers on family member and caregiver health-related quality of life from a healthcare system or health payer perspective, so impacts on others, wider welfare effects and interactions with broadly incurred costs were not fully examined.
The task force did not differentiate first-order from second-order spillovers, and gave limited consideration to cascade effects from shared genetic information.
Consultation with patients and caregivers was restricted to the later stages of the process, which may have limited the potential for their input to shape discussions.
